title: SYSK Selects: Why can't we find Amelia Earhart?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the December 2000 episode "Why Can't We Find Amelia Earhart?", reintroduced by Josh as a response to a recent photo purporting to show Earhart and Fred Noonan after their disappearance. The episode covers Earhart's career, the 1937 equatorial world flight, the final flight from Papua New Guinea toward Howland Island, the failed US Navy search, the 1940 Gardner Island (Nikumaroro) evidence including the bones taken by Gerald Gallagher's physician, the artifacts later found by TIGAR, and theories including Japanese capture, the Irene Craig alleged-identity claim, and a plane sunk in the Pacific. The episode ends with a listener mail about a rehab hospital experience.
rerun_of: Why Can't We Find Amelia Earhart?

segments.title: Selects introduction and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode, explaining it was chosen because of a recent photo purporting to show Earhart and Noonan after their disappearance. Hosts then trade light banter about Time Life books and the Greatest Mysteries of All Time list.

segments.title: Competing theories about Earhart's fate
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Japanese capture theory and the Tokyo Rose connection, and the alleged identity of Irene Craig Bolam, a claim that Earhart lived as a New Jersey housewife, which led to a lawsuit.

segments.title: Fred Noonan and Earhart's background
segments.summary: Noonan is described as the navigator with a traditional look. Earhart's pacifism, women's rights advocacy, and honors such as the Flying Cross and the National Geographic award are discussed, along with her earlier record flights.

segments.title: The 1937 equatorial round-the-world flight
segments.summary: The hosts explain the attempt to circumnavigate the globe along the equator and the Papua New Guinea departure. The Howland Island leg was the most dangerous, with a Coast Guard cutter Itasca and support ships stationed to help. Overcast weather blocked celestial navigation, and the last transmissions were received.

segments.title: Navy search and the Gardner Island lead
segments.summary: President Roosevelt ordered a massive multinational search covering about a quarter million square miles, which found nothing and drew criticism over cost. Later radio transmissions were heard near Gardner Island, prompting a destroyer dispatch, which also found nothing.

segments.title: Gardner Island artifacts and the bones
segments.summary: After British colonization of Gardner Island, settlers found evidence of a castaway, including shoes, a bottle, a sextant container, and human remains. Gerald Gallagher's physician took notes on the bones, which were later lost. Forensic anthropologists in the 1990s judged from the notes that the bones were a woman of Northern European ancestry about five foot seven. Other items such as cooking evidence and a knife blade were also found.

segments.title: TIGAR expeditions, DNA testing, and the plane in the ocean
segments.summary: TIGAR's expeditions found more items, including aluminum folk art and a knife, and submitted touch DNA samples for testing. The hosts discuss the possibility that the Electra survived largely intact on the ocean floor, and that ground penetrating radar found nothing conclusive.

segments.title: Speculation on the castaway's final days and closing notes
segments.summary: The hosts speculate about how long Earhart survived on Gardner Island and what she might have left behind, then close the topic by noting that the show will not likely update the episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: rehab hospital experience from Scott
segments.summary: Scott describes being hospitalized in 2005 after burnout, including a seventy-two hour hold, eight days at a locked psychiatric unit, and a twenty-eight day program. He reports on his experiences and says he is doing well now.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to send mail, share on Facebook and Twitter, and visit the Kiva and Coed links, and point to the HowStuffWorks site for more on Earhart.
